routes.label: Find a common divisor and prove maximality

question: What is the largest integer that is a divisor of \[ \begin{aligned} &(n + 1)(n + 3)(n + 5) \\ &\quad {}\cdot (n + 7)(n + 9) \end{aligned} \] for all positive even integers \(n?\)
solution:
Let \(P(n)=(n+1)(n+3)(n+5)(n+7)(n+9)\). Since \(n\) is even, the factors are five consecutive odd integers. We must find a divisor that always occurs, then rule out every larger divisor.

Adding \(2\) repeatedly cycles through the remainders \(0,2,1\) when dividing by \(3\), starting at whichever remainder the first factor has. Thus the first three factors include a multiple of \(3\). Similarly, adding \(2\) cycles through the five remainders \(0,2,4,1,3\) when dividing by \(5\), so the five factors include a multiple of \(5\). Because \(3\) and \(5\) are distinct primes, every allowed product is divisible by \(15\).

To bound a divisor common to all the products, it is enough to compare two carefully chosen allowed inputs. We have
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(10)&=11\cdot13\cdot15\cdot17\cdot19\\
&=3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(22)&=23\cdot25\cdot27\cdot29\cdot31\\
&=3^3\cdot5^2\cdot23\cdot29\cdot31.
\end{aligned}
\]
The only primes appearing in both factorizations are \(3\) and \(5\), and each appears only once in \(P(10)\). Therefore these two products have greatest common factor \(15\). Any positive integer dividing every allowed product must divide both of these, so it cannot exceed \(15\).

Since \(15\) divides every allowed product and no larger integer can do so, the answer is \(\boxed{15}\), choice D.
